acceptedAnswer.text: ArrayList is a resizable array implementation of the List interface in Java's Collections Framework, available in java.util package since Java 1.2. Unlike a plain array whose size is fixed at creation, ArrayList dynamically grows and shrinks as elements are added or removed. It stores elements in insertion order, allows duplicates, and permits null values. ArrayList is the most commonly used List implementation in Java for single-threaded applications.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between ArrayList and Array in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An Array in Java has a fixed size set at creation and cannot be resized. ArrayList is dynamic — it automatically grows when elements exceed capacity. Arrays can store both primitives and objects; ArrayList stores only objects (primitives are autoboxed). Arrays use array[index] syntax; ArrayList uses get(index) and add() methods. ArrayList implements the List interface and integrates with the Collections Framework; arrays do not. For most use cases requiring a resizable sequence, ArrayList is preferred over plain arrays.

No, ArrayList is not thread-safe. Its methods are not synchronized. If multiple threads access and modify an ArrayList concurrently, it can lead to data corruption or ConcurrentModificationException. For thread-safe alternatives, use Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()), CopyOnWriteArrayList from java.util.concurrent, or Vector (legacy). For single-threaded code, ArrayList is the fastest and most commonly used List implementation.

mainEntity.name: How does ArrayList grow internally in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: ArrayList starts with a default initial capacity of 10. When elements are added beyond the current capacity, ArrayList creates a new internal array with a capacity of approximately 1.5x the old capacity (newCapacity = oldCapacity + oldCapacity >> 1). All existing elements are copied to the new array via Arrays.copyOf(). This grow-on-demand strategy amortizes the cost of resizing over many add operations, giving ArrayList an amortized O(1) time complexity for add().

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?

acceptedAnswer.text: ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array — O(1) random access (get/set by index) but O(n) for insertions/deletions in the middle. LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list — O(n) random access but O(1) for insertions/deletions at the head or tail. ArrayList uses less memory per element (no node pointers). LinkedList also implements Deque, making it suitable as a queue or deque. For most read-heavy workloads, ArrayList outperforms LinkedList.

sections.title: What is the Java ArrayList Class?

blocks.text: The ArrayList class in Java is a part of the java.util package and provides a resizable (dynamic) array implementation of the List interface. It is the most widely used collection class in Java — the go-to choice whenever you need an ordered, index-accessible list of elements whose size is not known in advance.

Unlike a plain Java array — which has a fixed size set at creation — an ArrayList automatically grows its internal array when elements are added beyond current capacity, and can shrink it when needed. It preserves insertion order, allows duplicate elements, and permits null values. All elements are accessible by zero-based integer index in O(1) time.

Think of an ArrayList as a smart, elastic shelf. You can keep adding books (elements) to it — when it runs out of space, it quietly moves everything to a bigger shelf. You can reach any book instantly by its position number (index), and the shelf always knows exactly how many books it holds.
The ArrayList class provides three constructors. Always use generics (ArrayList<Type>) to ensure type safety and avoid raw-type warnings.

blocks.text: ArrayList is the default choice for most Java list operations. Here is why it dominates everyday Java development:

items.text: — No need to declare size upfront. ArrayList grows on demand. This eliminates ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from under-sized fixed arrays and memory waste from over-sized ones.
— Backed by an array, ArrayList provides O(1) get(index) and set(index) — as fast as a plain array. Perfect for workloads that read by index far more than they insert or delete.
— ArrayList implements java.util.List completely, making it compatible with Collections utility methods (sort, shuffle, binarySearch, reverse, frequency, disjoint) and all Java APIs expecting a List.
— Supports for-each, traditional for loop, Iterator, ListIterator, and Java 8+ streams — giving flexibility to choose the best traversal approach for each situation.
— ArrayList<T> enforces type safety at compile time. You cannot accidentally add a String to an ArrayList<Integer>, catching bugs before runtime.
— Built-in methods for add, remove, search (contains, indexOf, lastIndexOf), bulk operations (addAll, removeAll, retainAll, containsAll), subList, and conversion to array.
— Virtually every Java framework (Spring, Hibernate, Jackson, JAX-RS) works with List and returns or accepts ArrayList. It is the universal currency of Java data passing.

blocks.text: Choosing the right data structure depends on your access patterns, thread requirements, and whether size is known upfront. This table covers all four common options:

Decision guide: Use ArrayList by default for single-threaded ordered lists. Use LinkedList only if you frequently insert/delete at both ends. Use int[] arrays for primitive numeric data with fixed size. Avoid Vector in new code — use Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()) instead.

blocks.text: The flowchart below shows exactly what happens inside ArrayList when you call add(element) — how it decides whether to grow and how it calculates the new capacity.

Growth formula: newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1) — this is an arithmetic right shift by 1, equivalent to adding 50% of the current capacity. So a capacity-10 ArrayList grows to 15, then 22, then 33, then 49, and so on. This amortizes the O(n) copy cost across many insertions, giving add() an amortized O(1) time complexity.

blocks.text: Writing clean, efficient ArrayList code requires following these industry-standard best practices used in professional Java development:

items.text: — Always declare ArrayList variables as List<T> not ArrayList<T>. For example: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(). This decouples your code from the specific implementation, making it easy to swap to LinkedList or CopyOnWriteArrayList without changing callers.

items.strong: ✅ 2. Specify Initial Capacity When Size Is Known
items.text: — If you expect approximately N elements, construct with new ArrayList<>(N). This prevents multiple internal resize-and-copy cycles, improving performance for large lists. This is especially important in loops that add thousands of elements.

items.strong: ✅ 3. Always Use Generics — Never Raw Types
items.text: — List list = new ArrayList() is a raw type and bypasses compile-time type checking. Always use List<String> list = new ArrayList<>() to catch type mismatch bugs at compile time, not at runtime.

items.strong: ✅ 4. Use Iterator or removeIf() for Deletion During Traversal
items.text: — Never remove elements inside a for-each loop — it throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use Iterator.remove() for conditional removal during traversal, or the cleaner Java 8+ list.removeIf(predicate) for batch removal.

— When passing a list to external code that should not modify it, wrap it: Collections.unmodifiableList(myList). Any modification attempt throws UnsupportedOperationException immediately, preventing accidental mutation.

items.strong: ✅ 6. Prefer List.of() for Fixed Immutable Lists
items.text: — For a list of known constants that will never change, Java 9+ List.of("A", "B", "C") creates a compact, immutable list faster than constructing an ArrayList. Never use List.of() when you need to add or remove elements later.

items.strong: ✅ 7. Use Stream API for Filter/Map/Collect Pipelines
items.text: — For transformations (filtering, mapping, grouping), streams are more readable and often more performant than manual loops over ArrayList. Prefer list.stream().filter().map().collect() over imperative for-loops for such operations.
— Inserting at the beginning of an ArrayList is O(n) because all existing elements must shift right. For frequent head insertions or removals, use LinkedList or ArrayDeque instead.

ArrayList is the most versatile and widely used collection in Java — but it is not the right tool for every job. Understanding its trade-offs helps you choose correctly.

pros.title: O(1) Random Access
pros.text: Backed by an array, get(index) and set(index) are O(1) — as fast as a native array. Perfect for index-heavy workloads like lookup tables and paginated results.

pros.title: Dynamic Sizing
pros.text: No need to declare size upfront. ArrayList handles all internal resizing transparently, eliminating ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from size mismatch.

pros.title: Full Collections Framework Integration
pros.text: Implements List completely and works with all Collections utility methods — sort, binarySearch, shuffle, reverse, frequency, disjoint — and all Java APIs that accept List.

pros.title: Generics Type Safety
pros.text: ArrayList<T> catches type errors at compile time. You cannot accidentally store a wrong type, preventing ClassCastException at runtime.

pros.title: Versatile Iteration
pros.text: Supports six distinct traversal strategies — for loop, for-each, Iterator, ListIterator, forEach lambda, and Stream API — covering every traversal pattern cleanly.

pros.title: Rich Java 8+ API
pros.text: removeIf(), replaceAll(), sort(), stream(), and forEach() turn ArrayList into a powerful functional collection with minimal boilerplate for filtering, mapping, and transforming data.

pros.title: Memory Efficient
pros.text: Stores only element references in a contiguous array. No per-element overhead (unlike LinkedList's prev/next node pointers), giving compact memory layout and better CPU cache performance.

cons.title: Not Thread-Safe
cons.text: ArrayList is not synchronized. Concurrent access from multiple threads without external synchronization causes data corruption or ConcurrentModificationException. Use CopyOnWriteArrayList or Collections.synchronizedList() for multi-threaded scenarios.

cons.title: O(n) Middle Insertions and Deletions
cons.text: Inserting or deleting at any index other than the end requires shifting all subsequent elements — O(n). For workloads with frequent middle insertions, LinkedList is faster.

cons.title: O(n) Insertions at Index 0
cons.text: Prepending to the beginning shifts every element right — the most expensive write operation. If you frequently add to or remove from the head, use ArrayDeque or LinkedList instead.

cons.title: Wasted Capacity After Resizing
cons.text: After each growth cycle, approximately 33% of allocated capacity may be empty. Use trimToSize() or a carefully chosen initial capacity to avoid memory waste in large lists.

cons.title: No Primitive Storage — Autoboxing Overhead
cons.text: ArrayList<Integer> stores Integer objects, not int primitives. Autoboxing and unboxing incur object allocation overhead per element. For large primitive collections, use int[] arrays or IntStream.

cons.title: Fail-Fast Iterator
cons.text: ArrayList's Iterator throws ConcurrentModificationException if the list is structurally modified during iteration by anything other than Iterator.remove(). This trips up beginners who delete inside for-each loops.

blocks.text: These are the most frequently asked interview questions on Java ArrayList for Java developer, backend engineer, and SDET positions.

items.q: Q1. What is ArrayList in Java and how is it different from a plain array?
items.a: ArrayList is a resizable List implementation backed by a dynamic array. A plain array has a fixed size set at creation — you cannot add or remove elements. ArrayList grows automatically. Arrays can store primitives; ArrayList stores only objects (primitives are autoboxed). ArrayList implements the List interface and integrates with the Collections Framework; arrays do not. ArrayList provides rich built-in methods (sort, contains, indexOf, removeIf, stream) that arrays lack.

items.q: Q2. What is the default initial capacity of ArrayList and how does it grow?
items.a: The default initial capacity is 10. When elements exceed capacity, ArrayList creates a new internal array using the formula: newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1), which is approximately 1.5x (50% growth). All existing elements are copied to the new array via Arrays.copyOf(). This amortizes the resize cost, giving add() an amortized O(1) time complexity.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
items.a: ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array — O(1) get/set by index, O(n) insert/delete at middle. LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list — O(n) get by index, O(1) insert/delete at head or tail. ArrayList is more memory-efficient per element (no node pointers). LinkedList also implements Deque. For most use cases (read-heavy, index access), ArrayList outperforms LinkedList. Use LinkedList only for frequent head/tail insertions.

items.q: Q4. Is ArrayList thread-safe? How do you make it thread-safe?
items.a: ArrayList is NOT thread-safe. For thread safety: (1) Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()) — wraps ArrayList with synchronization on every method; (2) CopyOnWriteArrayList from java.util.concurrent — creates a new copy of the array on every write, making reads completely lock-free; best for read-heavy scenarios. (3) Use explicit synchronized blocks around compound operations. Vector is also thread-safe but is a legacy class.

items.q: Q5. What is ConcurrentModificationException and when does it occur with ArrayList?
items.a: ConcurrentModificationException is thrown when ArrayList's Iterator detects that the list was structurally modified (elements added or removed) since the iterator was created — through any means other than Iterator.remove(). This most commonly happens when elements are removed inside a for-each loop. Fix: use Iterator explicitly with it.remove(), or use list.removeIf(predicate) for batch removal.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between remove(int index) and remove(Object o) in ArrayList?
items.a: remove(int index) removes the element at the specified zero-based index and returns the removed element. remove(Object o) removes the first occurrence of the specified object and returns a boolean. For ArrayList<Integer>, calling remove(2) removes the element at index 2, NOT the Integer value 2. To remove the value 2, use remove(Integer.valueOf(2)). This is a common interview trap and a real-world bug source.

items.q: Q7. What does subList() return and what are its risks?
items.a: subList(fromIndex, toIndex) returns a view of the portion of the list between fromIndex (inclusive) and toIndex (exclusive). The returned list is backed by the original — modifications to the subList reflect in the original list and vice versa. If the original list is structurally modified (not through the subList), subsequent operations on the subList throw ConcurrentModificationException. To get an independent copy: new ArrayList<>(list.subList(from, to)).

items.q: Q8. What is the time complexity of contains() in ArrayList?
items.a: O(n) — linear scan. ArrayList does not maintain any index structure (like a HashSet or TreeSet). contains(o) iterates through all elements comparing each with equals(). For O(1) average-case lookup, use HashSet. If you frequently check membership AND need indexed access, maintain both an ArrayList (for ordering) and a HashSet (for fast lookup) together.

items.q: Q9. How is ArrayList different from Vector?
items.a: Both are dynamic array implementations of List. Key differences: (1) Vector is synchronized (thread-safe); ArrayList is not. (2) Vector doubles capacity on resize; ArrayList grows by ~50%. (3) Vector is a legacy class from Java 1.0; ArrayList was introduced in Java 1.2 as part of the Collections Framework. (4) ArrayList is faster in single-threaded scenarios due to no synchronization overhead. In modern code, ArrayList is always preferred; Vector is considered legacy.

items.q: Q10. What is the difference between List.of() and new ArrayList<>() in Java?
items.a: List.of() (Java 9+) creates a compact, immutable list — you cannot add, remove, or set elements; attempting throws UnsupportedOperationException. It also does not allow null elements. new ArrayList<>() creates a mutable, growable list that accepts nulls and allows all CRUD operations. Use List.of() for fixed constants and configuration values. Use new ArrayList<>() whenever the list needs to be modified after creation.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of ArrayList with these practice questions. Attempt each before revealing the answer.

items.q: 1. What is the capacity of an ArrayList after adding 16 elements to a default-constructed ArrayList?
items.a: 22. Default capacity is 10. After the 11th element, it grows: 10 + (10>>1) = 15. After the 16th element exceeds 15, it grows again: 15 + (15>>1) = 22. So after 16 adds, capacity = 22, size = 16.
[A, C]. remove(1) removes the element at index 1, which is "B". The list shifts: "C" moves to index 1. Result: [A, C].

items.q:
3. Why does this code throw ConcurrentModificationException and how do you fix it?
for (String s : list) { if (s.equals("X")) list.remove(s); }
items.a: For-each uses ArrayList's fail-fast Iterator internally. When list.remove(s) structurally modifies the list during iteration, the Iterator's modCount check fails and throws ConcurrentModificationException. Fix: use list.removeIf(s -> s.equals("X")), or use an explicit Iterator: Iterator<String> it = list.iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { if (it.next().equals("X")) it.remove(); }

items.q: 4. What is the difference in behavior: list.remove(2) vs list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)) on an ArrayList<Integer>?
items.a: list.remove(2) calls remove(int index) — removes the element at index 2 (the third element). list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)) calls remove(Object o) — searches for and removes the first element whose value equals Integer 2. For ArrayList<Integer>, always use Integer.valueOf() when removing by value to avoid accidental index-based removal.

items.q: 5. You have an ArrayList of 1 million elements. Describe the performance of: (a) get(500000), (b) add("X") at end, (c) add(0, "X") at beginning, (d) contains("X") — explain Big-O for each.
items.a: (a) O(1) — direct index access to internal array, same as array[500000]. (b) Amortized O(1) — no shift needed; occasional O(n) resize cost is amortized. (c) O(n) — 1 million elements must shift right by one position; most expensive ArrayList operation. (d) O(n) — linear scan through all 1 million elements comparing with equals(); use HashSet for O(1) lookup.

items.q: 6. What is the output? List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1,2,3,4,5)); List<Integer> b = a.subList(1,4); b.set(0, 99); System.out.println(a);
items.a: [1, 99, 3, 4, 5]. subList(1,4) returns a view backed by the original list [2,3,4] (indices 1,2,3). b.set(0,99) sets position 0 of the sublist view, which corresponds to index 1 of the original list. Since it is a view (not a copy), the change reflects directly in list a.

items.q: 7. What happens when you call Collections.sort() on an ArrayList of custom objects that do not implement Comparable?
items.a: Collections.sort() requires list elements to implement java.lang.Comparable or a Comparator to be provided. If neither is provided and elements don't implement Comparable, a ClassCastException is thrown at runtime when elements are compared. Fix: either implement Comparable<T> in the class (define natural ordering via compareTo()), or provide a Comparator: Collections.sort(list, Comparator.comparing(obj -> obj.field)).

items.q: 8. Can an ArrayList hold different types of objects simultaneously? Is it good practice?
items.a: Yes, using a raw ArrayList (without generics): ArrayList list = new ArrayList(); list.add("String"); list.add(42); list.add(3.14); — all compile without error. However this is terrible practice: it defeats compile-time type safety, requires casting on retrieval (error-prone), and triggers unchecked warnings. Always use generics: ArrayList<String>, ArrayList<Integer>, etc. If you genuinely need mixed types, use ArrayList<Object> with instanceof checks — or better, rethink your design.

blocks.text: ArrayList is the workhorse of Java development — the first data structure you reach for when you need an ordered, indexed, dynamically-sized collection. Its combination of O(1) random access, rich API, seamless generics support, and full Collections Framework integration makes it the correct default choice for the vast majority of Java list use cases.

Mastering ArrayList means knowing not just how to use it, but when not to: use LinkedList when you frequently insert at both ends, use CopyOnWriteArrayList when reads dominate in a multi-threaded context, use int[] when you need a large primitive array without boxing overhead, and use List.of() when immutability is a requirement.

Remember: Declare as List, instantiate as ArrayList, specify initial capacity when size is known, never modify during for-each, and always use generics. These five habits will keep your ArrayList code correct, performant, and production-ready. ☕
